cues.text: From Cathedral Schools to Universities
Medieval education before the twelfth century centered on monastic and cathedral schools, which preserved classical learning through the turmoil following Rome's fall.
As Europe stabilized and towns grew in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, some of these schools expanded rapidly.
Especially those attached to great cathedrals drew masters and students from across Christendom, gradually organizing themselves into self-governing corporations, or universitates .
Bologna and the Study of Law
The earliest of these, at Bologna , grew out of schools of the liberal arts flourishing in the early eleventh century.
By the twelfth, it had developed into Europe's leading center for studying Roman and canon law, following the influential legal compilation known as Gratian's Decretum .
Uniquely, Bologna's students themselves formed the primary corporate body, hiring and paying their own masters — a structure later copied by universities across Southern Europe.
Paris and the Rise of Scholastic Theology

In Paris, the schools of Notre-Dame, Sainte-Geneviève, and Saint-Victor combined by the mid-twelfth century into what became the University of Paris , the great center of theological and philosophical study in the Latin West.
Here, thinkers such as Peter Abelard sharpened the dialectical methods that would flower into full scholasticism .
Later masters, above all St. Thomas Aquinas in the following century, would produce the great theological syntheses of the High Middle Ages.
Oxford, Cambridge, and Beyond

England's Oxford emerged as a center of study in the late twelfth century, populated partly by scholars returning from Paris, and Cambridge followed after a dispute drove masters away from Oxford in the early thirteenth century.
By the thirteenth century, formal papal and royal charters had spread this Parisian and Bolognese model to Prague, Vienna, Salamanca, and beyond.
These charters granted universities corporate legal standing, the right to award licenses to teach anywhere, and considerable independence from local authorities.
The Church's Formative Role
Nearly every early university depended on the Church for its legitimacy, funding, and personnel.
The licentia docendi, or license to teach, was originally an ecclesiastical grant.

Most professors and students belonged to the clergy in some capacity (however minor), and popes repeatedly intervened, as at Bologna, to standardize degree requirements and extend a doctor's right to teach across all of Christendom.
Legacy
The medieval university created the basic institutional structure of higher learning still recognizable today — faculties, degrees, examinations, and a canon of required texts.
It became the engine that produced the great scholastic synthesis of faith and reason associated with figures like Aquinas and Bonaventure.
Nearly every later European university, and by extension the entire modern research university, traces its lineage to this Church-nurtured innovation of the twelfth century.
